title: Git Internals
tagline: Understand Git's object model — blobs, trees, commits, and the DAG — so merges, rebases, and refs are never magic again.

sections.content:
Most developers treat Git as a black box: `git add`, `git commit`, `git push`, and pray. When something goes wrong — a detached HEAD, a failed rebase, a 'not a fast-forward' error — they reach for Stack Overflow rather than understanding what actually happened. But Git's apparent complexity is a facade over a remarkably elegant design. Once you see the underlying structure, those cryptic error messages stop being scary and start being informative.

At its core, Git is a **content-addressable object store** sitting inside the `.git` directory of every repository. Every piece of data Git tracks is stored as one of exactly four object types: a **blob** (raw file content), a **tree** (directory listing), a **commit** (snapshot plus metadata), or a **tag** (annotated pointer). Every object is identified by the SHA-1 hash of its own content — two objects with the same hash are guaranteed to be identical; two objects with different hashes are guaranteed to be different.

Built on top of that object store is a **Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)** of commits. Each commit points to its parent commit (or two parents in a merge), forming a chain of snapshots stretching back to the very first commit. Because the graph only flows forward in time and never forms cycles, the term 'directed acyclic' is technically precise. **Refs** — branches, tags, and `HEAD` — are nothing more than human-readable names that point to specific nodes in that graph. A branch is a sticky note on a commit; `git commit` moves the sticky note forward automatically.

Finally, sitting between your working directory and the object store is the **staging area** (also called the index): a prepared snapshot you build up with `git add` before crystallising it into a commit. Understanding these three ideas — content-addressable object store, commit DAG, and refs as lightweight pointers — demystifies every advanced Git operation. Merge conflicts, rebases, cherry-picks, reflog recovery: they all become logical consequences of a simple data model you can reason about from first principles.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    WD["Working Directory\nfiles on disk"]
    IDX["Staging Area / Index\nnext snapshot draft"]
    OBJ["Object Store\n.git/objects"]
    BLOB["blob\nraw file content"]
    TREE["tree\ndirectory listing"]
    CMT["commit\ntree + parent + message"]
    REF["refs / HEAD\nnamed pointers"]
    WD -->|"git add"| IDX
    IDX -->|"git commit"| OBJ
    OBJ --> BLOB
    OBJ --> TREE
    OBJ --> CMT
    CMT -->|"pointed to by"| REF
sections.caption: Git's three-stage architecture: working directory feeds into the staging area, which crystallises into the object store. Refs are lightweight pointers into the commit DAG.

sections.title: A Library with Immutable, Fingerprinted Books
sections.content:
Imagine a very unusual library. Every book receives a unique catalogue number derived by computing a fingerprint of its exact content — change even one character in the book, and it gets a completely different number. Two identical books share one catalogue slot. This is Git's **object store**: every file snapshot and directory snapshot is stored exactly once, identified by a SHA-1 fingerprint of its bytes. Identical content across twenty branches takes up storage space of just one copy.

A **commit** is like a dated catalogue card: 'On 3 January 2024, the shelf arrangement looked exactly like *this tree* (identified by catalogue number XYZ), and it followed on from the arrangement described in card *ABC* (the parent commit).' The **commit DAG** is the full archive of those catalogue cards, each pointing back to the card it was derived from. You can trace any card backwards to the very first one, but you can never introduce a cycle — history only flows in one direction.

**Branches** are sticky notes you press onto a card. When you check out a branch and make a new commit, Git writes a new card and moves your sticky note forward to it automatically. **HEAD** is a special meta-sticky-note that says 'I am currently looking at *this* note.' When you `git checkout feature`, HEAD points to the feature branch's sticky note. When that branch's note moves, HEAD follows. In 'detached HEAD' state, HEAD points directly to a card rather than to a sticky note — you are browsing history without a branch to move forward.

**The staging area** is your scratchpad before you write a new card. You gather the books (files) you want to include, arrange them on the staging shelf with `git add`, and then `git commit` photographs the shelf and writes the card. You can stage parts of changes, amend the arrangement, and only commit when you are satisfied — the working directory and the commit are always separated by this intentional staging step.

sections.title: The Four Object Types: Blobs, Trees, Commits, Tags
sections.content:
Everything Git stores is one of four object types. Understanding each type precisely is the key to understanding all Git behaviour.

**Blobs** are the simplest type: a blob stores raw file content and nothing else. No filename. No path. No permissions. Just bytes. The SHA-1 of a blob is computed from the string `blob <length>\0<content>`. Because the identity is derived from content alone, two files in completely different directories with identical content produce exactly one blob object. This is how Git achieves storage efficiency without explicit deduplication logic — deduplication is a mathematical consequence of content-addressing.

**Trees** represent directories. A tree object contains a list of entries, where each entry has three fields: a **mode** (file permissions, like `100644` for a regular file or `040000` for a subdirectory), a **name** (the filename or directory name), and a **SHA-1** pointing to either a blob (for a file) or another tree (for a subdirectory). Crucially, a tree does not store file contents directly — it just points to blobs. And because trees are also content-addressed, an unchanged subdirectory's tree SHA stays the same across commits. Git only writes new tree objects for directories that actually changed.

**Commits** are the objects most developers are familiar with, but their internal structure is worth knowing precisely. A commit object contains: a pointer to the **root tree** (the top-level directory snapshot), one or more **parent commit** SHA-1s (zero for the initial commit, one normally, two or more for merge commits), **author** name/email/timestamp, **committer** name/email/timestamp (can differ from author after rebasing or cherry-picking), and the **commit message**. The commit's own SHA-1 is derived from all of this content. Change anything — even the message, even the timestamp — and you get a different SHA-1. This is why every `git rebase` or `git commit --amend` produces new SHA-1 hashes: the parent pointer changes, so the hash changes, even if the tree (and therefore the file contents) are identical.

**Tags** come in two varieties. A **lightweight tag** is simply a refs file pointing to a commit SHA — no object is created. An **annotated tag** creates an actual `tag` object in the object store containing: the target object's SHA-1, the target type (usually 'commit'), the tag name, the tagger identity, a timestamp, and a message. Annotated tags can be GPG-signed, making them cryptographically verified release markers. Use annotated tags for releases; lightweight tags for temporary local bookmarks.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    C["commit object\ntree: abc123\nparent: def456\nauthor: Ada"]
    T["tree object\nREADME.md -> blob 111\nsrc/ -> tree 222"]
    B1["blob 111\nRaw README content"]
    T2["tree 222\nmain.js -> blob 333"]
    B2["blob 333\nRaw main.js content"]
    C --> T
    T --> B1
    T --> T2
    T2 --> B2
sections.caption: A single commit points to a root tree. The tree points to blobs (files) and sub-trees (subdirectories). Every object is identified by its SHA-1 hash.

sections.title: The Commit DAG: History as a Graph
sections.content:
A **Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)** is a structure where each node points to one or more other nodes, the edges have direction, and you cannot follow a path that loops back to its starting point. Git's commit history is precisely such a structure: each commit points to its parent commit(s), edges run from child to parent (forward in time), and since time does not run backward, there are no cycles.

Most commits have exactly one parent — the previous commit on a linear development line. The **initial commit** has no parent (it is the root of the DAG). A **merge commit** has two or more parents — one for each branch being merged. This is what makes the DAG non-linear at merge points: the graph branches out (when development diverges) and converges again (when branches merge).

The DAG structure has profound consequences. First, **history is immutable**: because a commit's SHA-1 encodes its parent's SHA-1, changing any ancestor commit would change all descendant SHA-1s as well. The entire chain must change. This means `git rebase` and `git commit --amend` do not edit history — they create new commits alongside the old ones. The old commits remain in the object store, accessible via `git reflog`, until garbage collection removes them.

Second, **branching is free**: creating a branch is just creating a new file in `.git/refs/heads/` containing a SHA-1. No data is copied. No objects are created. A thousand branches cost kilobytes of storage.

Third, **common history is shared**: if two branches share the first hundred commits, both branches reference exactly the same hundred commit objects, blob objects, and tree objects. No duplication occurs. Storage scales with the number of unique objects, not with the number of branches.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
    A["commit A\ninitial"]
    B["commit B\nmain work"]
    C["commit C\nfeature work"]
    M["merge commit M\nparents: B and C"]
    R["commit C-prime\nrebased onto B"]
    A --> B
    A --> C
    B --> M
    C --> M
    B --> R
sections.caption: Merge (left path) creates a two-parent merge commit M preserving full non-linear history. Rebase (right path) replays C as C-prime on top of B — linear history but a new SHA-1, even if the diff is identical.

sections.title: Refs and HEAD: The Pointer System
sections.content:
With thousands of commit SHA-1 hashes in a repository, humans need named entry points into the graph. That is what refs provide.

**Branches** live in `.git/refs/heads/` as plain text files containing a single SHA-1 hash. The file `.git/refs/heads/main` might contain `a3f8e291...`. When you run `git commit`, Git writes a new commit object, then overwrites that file with the new commit's SHA-1. Branches are therefore **mutable pointers** that automatically advance as you commit. Creating a branch is just writing a new file; deleting a branch is just deleting that file. The commits the branch pointed to are unchanged.

**Remote-tracking refs** live in `.git/refs/remotes/` and represent the last-known state of branches on a remote. `origin/main` tells you where `main` was on the remote last time you fetched. These refs are read-only — Git updates them during `git fetch`/`git pull`, but you do not commit directly to them.

**HEAD** is the special pointer in `.git/HEAD` that tells Git which branch (or commit) you are currently on. Normally it contains an indirect reference like `ref: refs/heads/main` — this is called a **symbolic ref**. Git follows the indirection: HEAD -> main -> SHA-1. When you `git checkout main`, Git updates HEAD to point at main. When you commit, Git advances main, and HEAD follows automatically.

**Detached HEAD** occurs when HEAD contains a raw SHA-1 rather than a branch reference — typically after `git checkout <sha>` or `git checkout v1.0` (lightweight tag). In this state, commits you make do not advance any branch. If you switch away without creating a branch, those commits become unreachable and will eventually be garbage-collected. Git warns you explicitly about this state, which is why the message can seem alarming — but the solution is simple: `git checkout -b new-branch` to anchor your work to a new branch pointer.

**Tags** live in `.git/refs/tags/`. Unlike branches, tags do not move when you commit — they are **immutable pointers** intended to mark specific historical moments like releases.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
    HEAD["HEAD\nref: refs/heads/main"]
    MAIN["refs/heads/main\nSHA: a3f8e29"]
    FEAT["refs/heads/feature\nSHA: 91bc204"]
    CMT1["commit a3f8e29\nlatest main"]
    CMT2["commit 91bc204\nlatest feature"]
    CMT0["commit 5d12ab7\nshared ancestor"]
    HEAD --> MAIN
    MAIN --> CMT1
    FEAT --> CMT2
    CMT1 --> CMT0
    CMT2 --> CMT0
sections.caption: HEAD points to a branch ref, which points to a commit SHA. Both branches share the ancestor commit — no data duplication.

sections.title: The Staging Area (Index): Your Draft Snapshot
sections.content:
The **staging area** — also called the **index** — is one of Git's most misunderstood features, yet it is key to how Git achieves precise, well-crafted commits.

The index lives in the file `.git/index`. It is a binary file that represents a flat listing of every tracked file: the mode, SHA-1 blob hash, and filename for each file in the snapshot being prepared. It always contains a complete view of the working tree as you intend to commit it — not just the changed files, but all tracked files.

When you run `git add file.txt`, Git does two things: it **hashes the current content** of `file.txt` and writes a blob object into `.git/objects/`, then **updates the index** to point to that new blob SHA-1 for `file.txt`. The working directory copy of `file.txt` is unaffected.

When you subsequently edit `file.txt` again (without another `git add`), the index still points to the blob from the first `git add`. The working directory has moved on, but the staging area has not. This is why `git diff` shows the difference between working directory and index, while `git diff --cached` shows the difference between index and last commit — two separate gaps.

When you run `git commit`, Git reads the entire index, builds a tree object (and any necessary sub-tree objects) from the index entries, writes a commit object pointing to that tree and to the current HEAD commit as parent, then advances the current branch ref to the new commit SHA-1. At no point does `git commit` look at the working directory files directly.

This design enables powerful workflows: you can make multiple changes in your working directory but stage them selectively with `git add -p` (interactive patch mode), building separate focused commits from a messy work session. You can also use `git stash` to save and restore the working directory and index state as a special commit branch, letting you switch context without losing uncommitted work.

sections.label: Example
sections.code:
# ── Bootstrap a fresh repo and inspect every layer ──────────────
git init demo && cd demo
echo 'hello git' > hello.txt
git add hello.txt

# git add hashed hello.txt and stored it as a blob
git ls-files --stage
# 100644 8d0e41234f24b6da002d962a26c2495ea16a425f 0  hello.txt
#        ^ this is the blob SHA stored in the index

# Inspect the blob directly
git cat-file -t 8d0e41   # => blob
git cat-file -p 8d0e41   # => hello git

git commit -m "initial commit"

# Inspect the commit object
git cat-file -p HEAD
# tree  <tree-sha>
# author Ada Lovelace <ada@example.com> 1704067200 +0000
# committer Ada Lovelace <ada@example.com> 1704067200 +0000
#
# initial commit

# Inspect the tree the commit points to
git cat-file -p HEAD^{tree}
# 100644 blob 8d0e41...  hello.txt

# ── See what refs actually are on disk ─────────────────────────
cat .git/HEAD                  # ref: refs/heads/main
cat .git/refs/heads/main       # a3f8e291... (the commit SHA)

# ── The three-way diff: working dir vs index vs last commit ────
echo 'line 1' > file.txt
echo 'line 2' >> file.txt
git add file.txt               # stage both lines
echo 'line 3' >> file.txt      # add third line WITHOUT staging

git diff                       # working-dir vs index: shows line 3
git diff --cached              # index vs HEAD: shows lines 1-2
git commit -m "staged snapshot, not working dir"
# line 3 is NOT in the commit — the index was captured, not the file

# ── Detached HEAD walkthrough ──────────────────────────────────
git log --oneline              # abc1234 staged snapshot...
git checkout abc1234           # detached HEAD at abc1234
cat .git/HEAD                  # abc1234...  (raw SHA, not a branch!)
git checkout -b rescue-branch  # anchor work to a new branch
sections.explanation: `git cat-file -p` is your X-ray into the object store — it pretty-prints any blob, tree, commit, or tag by SHA-1 prefix. The three diff commands reveal the two gaps: working-dir-vs-index and index-vs-HEAD. Detached HEAD is visible by reading `.git/HEAD` directly — when it contains a raw SHA instead of `ref: refs/heads/...`, you are detached.

sections.title: Merge vs Rebase: Two Ways to Integrate Changes
sections.content:
Both `git merge` and `git rebase` integrate changes from one branch into another. They produce the same final file content — but they create fundamentally different graph structures, with different implications for SHA-1 stability, readability, and collaboration safety.

**How merge works:** `git merge feature` finds the **merge base** — the most recent common ancestor commit of the current branch and the feature branch. It then performs a three-way merge: comparing the merge base state with the tip of each branch. If changes do not conflict (they touch different lines or different files), Git combines them automatically. The result is a new **merge commit** with two parent pointers. This merge commit appears in history, and the full non-linear shape of the graph is preserved. `git log --graph` will show the two branches diverging and converging.

**How rebase works:** `git rebase main` does something more surgical. Git identifies the commits on your current branch that are not in main (the commits after the merge base). It then replays each of those commits, one by one, on top of the tip of main. For each commit, Git computes the diff from its parent, applies that diff to the new base, and creates a **new commit object** with the new parent SHA, the new tree, and (by default) the original author/message. The original commits still exist in the object store but are no longer reachable from any branch — they become orphans, eventually collected by `git gc`.

**The key trade-off:** Merge is safe to do on shared remote branches because it does not rewrite existing SHA-1s — other developers' local copies stay valid. Rebase rewrites SHA-1s, so if you rebase commits that a colleague has already based work on, their history diverges from yours and `git pull` will create a mess. This is the origin of the **golden rule of rebasing**: only rebase commits that exist exclusively in your local branch, never commits you have already pushed to a shared remote.

**When to use each:** Many teams use rebase to keep feature branches up to date with main (keeping the branch's history linear and easy to read), then merge with `--no-ff` when the feature is complete (to create a visible merge commit that marks the integration point). Other teams use squash merges, which flatten a branch's history into one commit before merging. The 'right' approach depends on team conventions, but knowing the mechanics lets you reason about any approach.

**Fast-forward merges** are a special case: if the current branch is a direct ancestor of the branch being merged (no divergence has occurred), Git can simply move the current branch pointer forward to the target commit — no merge commit is needed. This is what Git does by default when it can. `git merge --no-ff` forces a merge commit even in this case, preserving the record that a merge happened.

sections.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
    participant M as main
    participant F as feature
    participant G as git
    M->>G: tip commit B
    F->>G: tip commit C
    G->>G: find merge base A
    G->>G: three-way merge B + C vs A
    G->>M: write merge commit M with parents B and C
sections.caption: A three-way merge: Git finds the common ancestor A, compares each branch tip against A, and combines non-conflicting changes into merge commit M.

sections.label: Example
sections.code:
# ── Merge: preserves full history with a merge commit ──────────
git checkout -b feature main
echo 'feature work' > feature.txt
git add feature.txt && git commit -m "add feature work"

git checkout main
git merge feature            # creates a merge commit
git log --oneline --graph
# *   abc1234 Merge branch 'feature'
# |\  
# | * 91bc204 add feature work
# |/  
# *   5d12ab7 previous main work

# ── Rebase: replays commits for a linear history ───────────────
# Imagine feature has diverged from main after main got new commits
git checkout feature
git rebase main              # replays feature commits onto main tip
git log --oneline --graph
# * f9e8d7c add feature work   <- NEW SHA-1, same diff as before
# * 3a1b2c3 new main commit
# * 5d12ab7 previous main work

# ── Interactive rebase: rewrite history deliberately ───────────
# Squash last 3 commits into one clean commit:
git rebase -i HEAD~3
# Editor opens with:
# pick abc1234 wip
# pick def5678 more wip
# pick ghi9012 actually done
# Change to:
# pick abc1234 wip
# squash def5678 more wip
# squash ghi9012 actually done
# Git squashes all three into one commit with a combined message

# ── GOLDEN RULE: never rebase shared history ───────────────────
# After: git push origin feature
# Do NOT run: git rebase main && git push --force origin feature
# Other developers who fetched 'feature' now have a diverged history
# The safe workflow: merge main into feature, or accept the non-linear log
sections.explanation: The `--graph` flag on `git log` visually shows the DAG branching and merging. Interactive rebase (`-i`) is one of Git's most powerful tools: you can squash, reorder, edit, or drop commits to build a clean, logical history before sharing. The golden rule: once pushed to a remote others use, treat those commits as immutable.

sections.title: Reflog: The Time Machine Inside Git
sections.content:
The **reflog** (reference log) is one of Git's best-kept secrets and the reason 'I lost my commits' is almost always recoverable. Every time HEAD moves — from a checkout, a commit, a merge, a rebase, a reset — Git appends an entry to `.git/logs/HEAD` recording where HEAD was and where it moved to.

Reflog entries look like `HEAD@{0}`, `HEAD@{1}`, `HEAD@{2}` where `{0}` is the most recent state. You can also access branch-specific reflogs: `git reflog show main` shows every time main moved.

The classic recovery scenario: you run `git reset --hard HEAD~5` to undo five commits, then realise you needed those commits. Because the commits still exist in the object store (they are not immediately deleted), reflog lets you find their SHA-1s and recover them:

```
git reflog              # find the SHA before the reset
git checkout -b recovery-branch <sha>   # branch off that SHA
```

Reflog is **local only** — it is not shared when you push. Each developer has their own reflog for their own HEAD movements. Remote repositories typically have reflogs for their refs too, but you cannot access them directly with `git reflog`.

Reflog entries expire after 90 days by default (configurable via `gc.reflogExpire`). After expiry, unreachable commits become eligible for garbage collection via `git gc`. Before that window closes, `git reflog` is your safety net for almost any accidental destructive operation: hard resets, deleted branches, bad rebases.

sections.title: Packfiles and Storage Efficiency
sections.content:
When you first add a file to Git, it stores a loose object — a zlib-compressed file at a path derived from its SHA-1 (e.g., `.git/objects/ab/cdef1234...`). For small repositories with few commits, this is fine. But a repository with thousands of commits and many versions of large files would accumulate enormous numbers of loose objects, each storing a complete file snapshot.

Git's solution is **packfiles**. When Git runs garbage collection (`git gc`), or during `git fetch`/`git push` operations with many objects, Git groups loose objects into binary packfiles stored in `.git/objects/pack/`. Crucially, packfiles use **delta compression**: rather than storing every version of a file in full, the packfile stores one base version and a sequence of binary diffs (deltas) describing how to reconstruct subsequent versions. Blobs that are textually similar — like successive versions of the same source file — share a delta chain, making storage highly efficient.

This is why Git repositories are often surprisingly compact relative to the number of commits they contain: a file edited a thousand times does not require a thousand full copies. It requires one base and a chain of deltas.

Packfiles come with index files (`.idx`) that provide fast random access: given a SHA-1, the index lets Git locate the object in the packfile without scanning the entire pack. Multiple packfiles can exist simultaneously; `git gc` will consolidate them periodically.

One important implication: binary files (images, compiled artifacts, PDFs) do not delta-compress well, because binary formats change in ways that do not produce small deltas. This is why storing large binary files in Git is discouraged — it creates large packfiles without the compression benefit. Tools like Git LFS (Large File Storage) address this by storing large binaries externally and keeping only small pointer files in the Git object store.

sections.label: Example
sections.code:
# ── Reflog: recover anything ─────────────────────────────────────
git reflog
# HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~3
# HEAD@{1}: commit: add important feature
# HEAD@{2}: commit: fix critical bug  
# HEAD@{3}: commit: initial work

# Recover commits lost in a bad reset
git reset --hard HEAD@{1}       # undo the reset, back to the good commit
# OR create a recovery branch:
git checkout -b recovery HEAD@{1}

# ── Packfiles: inspect storage ───────────────────────────────────
# Count loose objects before gc
find .git/objects -type f | grep -v pack | wc -l

git gc                           # pack loose objects, prune reflog
ls .git/objects/pack/
# pack-abc123.idx
# pack-abc123.pack

# Verify pack contents
git verify-pack -v .git/objects/pack/pack-abc123.pack | head -20
# Shows each object: SHA type size compressed-size
# Delta entries show: SHA type size size-in-packfile offset depth base-SHA

# ── Annotated vs lightweight tags ────────────────────────────────
git tag v1.0-lightweight          # just a ref file, no object
git tag -a v1.0 -m "Release 1.0" # creates a tag object

git cat-file -t v1.0-lightweight  # commit  (points directly to commit)
git cat-file -t v1.0              # tag     (tag object with metadata)
git cat-file -p v1.0
# object 91bc204...
# type commit
# tag v1.0
# tagger Ada Lovelace <ada@example.com> 1704067200 +0000
#
# Release 1.0

# ── git stash internals ───────────────────────────────────────────
git stash                         # saves work as a hidden commit tree
git stash list
# stash@{0}: WIP on main: 5d12ab7 previous main work
cat .git/refs/stash               # a commit SHA — stash is just a commit!
sections.explanation: Reflog is a pure recovery tool — always try it before panicking about lost commits. `git verify-pack -v` lets you see the delta chains inside a packfile. The `git stash` internals reveal that stash is just commits stored off a special ref, not a separate storage mechanism — which means stashed work is also recoverable via reflog if you accidentally drop a stash.

sections.content: **SHA-1 and the transition to SHA-256:** Git has historically used SHA-1 as its object hash. SHA-1 is now considered cryptographically weak — chosen-prefix collision attacks are feasible. Git has two defenses: (1) the object store uses SHA-1 for deduplication and integrity, not authentication; (2) a collision-attack on Git would require constructing a pair of different commits with the same SHA-1, which while theoretically possible is extremely expensive in practice for an active repository. Nevertheless, the Git project has been working on a SHA-256 transition (the `object-format = sha256` repository setting) since 2020. Repositories using SHA-256 work identically conceptually — blobs, trees, commits, and refs still exist — but every hash is 64 hex characters instead of 40. The transition is backward-incompatible, so most hosted services still default to SHA-1.

**Common mistakes and interview insights:**

- **'Branches are cheap because...'** — the correct answer is that a branch is just a 41-byte text file (40-char SHA + newline). No objects are copied.
- **Rebase changes SHA-1 even with identical diffs** because the parent SHA is part of the commit object's content, and the hash is derived from the entire object. This is a favourite interview question.
- **`git commit --amend` is actually a rebase** — it creates a new commit with an updated message/tree and the same parent as HEAD, then moves HEAD to the new commit. The old commit still exists until garbage collection.
- **Detached HEAD is not broken** — it is a legitimate state for browsing history. The danger is only if you make commits you want to keep without first creating a branch.
- **`git reset --soft` vs `--mixed` vs `--hard`**: soft moves HEAD only (staged and working dir unchanged); mixed moves HEAD and resets the index (working dir unchanged); hard moves HEAD, resets the index, and overwrites the working directory — the only one that can lose work.
- **`git fetch` never changes your working directory** — it only updates remote-tracking refs. `git pull` is `git fetch` followed by `git merge` (or `git rebase` if configured).

items: **Git is a content-addressable object store**: blobs (file content), trees (directories), commits (snapshots + metadata), and tags are all stored by SHA-1 hash of their content — identical content is stored once, forever.

**Commits form an immutable DAG**: each commit encodes its parent's SHA-1, so any history rewrite (amend, rebase, cherry-pick) produces entirely new SHA-1 hashes — original commits remain in the object store until garbage collected.

**Branches and tags are lightweight ref files**: a branch is a text file in `.git/refs/heads/` containing a SHA-1; creating or deleting a branch touches no commit objects. HEAD points to a branch (normal) or directly to a commit (detached HEAD).

**The staging area (index) is your draft snapshot**: `git add` hashes content into the object store and updates the index; `git commit` reads the index to build a tree — the working directory is never read by commit directly.

**Merge preserves the full non-linear DAG** with a two-parent merge commit; **rebase replays commits linearly** with new SHA-1s — both integrate the same changes but produce different graph shapes. Never rebase shared remote history.
**Reflog is your safety net**: every HEAD movement is logged locally for 90 days, making almost every 'lost commit' recoverable with `git reflog` and `git checkout -b recovery <sha>`.

**Packfiles use delta compression** to keep repositories compact — successive versions of the same file share a delta chain rather than storing full copies, which is why text-based repositories stay small even with long histories.

quiz.question: What does a Git **blob** object store?
options: A directory listing mapping filenames to SHA-1 hashes
Raw file content, identified by the SHA-1 of that content alone
A snapshot of the entire repository at a point in time
Metadata about the author and timestamp of a change
quiz.explanation: A blob stores only raw file bytes — no filename, no path, no permissions. The SHA-1 is derived from the content, so two files with identical content share one blob object regardless of where they live in the directory tree.

quiz.question: Which fields are stored inside a Git **commit** object?
options: A compressed tarball of all changed files and a diff against the parent
A pointer to the root tree, parent commit SHA(s), author/committer info, and message
A list of staged files with their blob hashes and file permissions
The output of git diff --stat compared to the previous commit
quiz.explanation: A commit contains: root tree SHA, zero or more parent commit SHAs, author identity and timestamp, committer identity and timestamp, and message. Git computes diffs on demand by comparing trees — diffs are not stored.

quiz.question: You run `git add file.txt`, then edit `file.txt` again without a second `git add`. What does `git commit` record?
options: The latest on-disk version of file.txt including the second edit
No changes at all — Git detects the dirty file and aborts
The version of file.txt that was staged with the first `git add`
A merge of the staged version and the current on-disk version
quiz.explanation: `git commit` reads the index (staging area), not the working directory. The second edit is visible in `git diff` (working-dir vs index) but absent from `git diff --cached` (index vs HEAD), so only the first staged version is committed.

quiz.question: Why does `git rebase` produce new SHA-1 hashes even when the file changes are byte-for-byte identical to the original commits?
options: Rebase stores delta diffs instead of tree snapshots, changing the object format
Git randomly salts SHA-1 inputs during rebase to prevent duplicate hashes
The parent SHA-1 is part of the commit object's content, so a new parent changes the hash
Rebase compresses blobs differently from regular commits
quiz.explanation: A commit's SHA-1 is derived from all of its content: tree SHA, parent SHA(s), author, committer, timestamp, and message. Rebase places commits on a new parent, changing the parent SHA field, which changes the entire commit hash — even if the tree (file contents) is identical.

quiz.question: What is a Git branch, at the file-system level?
options: A separate copy of the repository's object store in a new directory
A compressed snapshot of the working tree at the branch creation point
A plain text file in `.git/refs/heads/` containing a single commit SHA-1
An index file listing all commits that belong to that branch
quiz.explanation: A branch is simply a file in `.git/refs/heads/` containing a 40-character SHA-1 hash (plus newline). No objects are copied. Creating a branch writes ~41 bytes; deleting one removes that file. This is why branches in Git are 'cheap'.

quiz.question: What distinguishes a merge commit from a regular commit in the object store?
options: A merge commit stores a unified diff of both branches instead of a tree snapshot
A merge commit has two or more parent SHA-1 pointers in its commit object
A merge commit is stored as a tag object rather than a commit object
A merge commit can only be created with the `--squash` flag
quiz.explanation: A merge commit is an ordinary commit object in every way except that it contains two or more parent SHA-1 pointers — one for each branch being merged. This is what makes the commit DAG non-linear at the merge point.

quiz.question: What is **detached HEAD** state in Git?
options: A state where the local HEAD ref is out of sync with the remote HEAD
A corrupted repository where `.git/HEAD` is missing or unreadable
A state where HEAD points directly to a commit SHA rather than to a branch ref
A state that occurs when two branches point to the same commit
quiz.explanation: Detached HEAD means `.git/HEAD` contains a raw commit SHA-1 instead of a symbolic ref like `ref: refs/heads/main`. Commits made in this state are not attached to any branch, and if you switch away without creating a branch, those commits become unreachable.

quiz.question: What is `git reflog` primarily used for?
options: Viewing the list of remote-tracking branches and their upstream URLs
Recovering commits that appear lost after a hard reset, bad rebase, or deleted branch
Displaying the full diff of the most recent commit
Listing all annotated tags and their signed checksums
quiz.explanation: Reflog records every HEAD movement locally with timestamps and descriptions. If you `reset --hard` too far, delete a branch, or make commits in detached HEAD then switch away, reflog shows the SHA-1 you were on before, letting you recover the work.

quiz.question: An annotated tag differs from a lightweight tag in that it:
options: Points to a branch ref instead of directly to a commit SHA
Is stored as its own tag object containing tagger name, date, and message
Moves forward automatically when new commits are made on that branch
Cannot be fetched or pushed to a remote repository
quiz.explanation: An annotated tag (`git tag -a`) creates an actual `tag` object in the object store with its own SHA-1, containing the target object SHA, tagger identity, timestamp, and message. A lightweight tag is just a ref file pointing directly to a commit — no tag object is created.

quiz.question: Which statement about Git packfiles is accurate?
options: Packfiles store only the latest version of each file, discarding older versions to save space
Packfiles delta-compress similar objects so successive versions of a file share a diff chain rather than full copies
Packfiles are created automatically on every `git commit` and replace loose objects immediately
Packfiles disable `git cat-file` because objects are no longer individually addressable by SHA-1
quiz.explanation: Packfiles use delta compression: similar blobs (like successive versions of the same file) are stored as one base object plus a chain of binary diffs. Packfiles are created by `git gc` or during network fetch/push operations — not on every commit. Objects remain fully addressable by SHA-1 via the packfile's `.idx` index.
